{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"The agent.png image illustrates that agents are typically implemented as an LLM performing actions using tools, operating in continuous feedback loops, and used in situations where problems and solutions are unpredictable.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"The image visually represents that agents have more autonomy than workflows and can make decisions about the tools they use and how to solve problems, while still allowing definition of the available toolset and guidelines for agent behavior.","citations":["c1"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"To use TrackingState with a node-style hook to update agent state after a model call, define a custom AgentState subclass with the desired state fields, such as model_call_count.","citations":["c1","c8"]},{"text":"Then, create an after_model node-style hook decorated with @after_model and specify the state_schema as TrackingState.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"Inside the after_model hook function, accept the current state and runtime as parameters and return a dictionary with the updated state fields, for example incrementing model_call_count by 1.","citations":["c1","c2"]},{"text":"The returned dictionary from the node-style hook is merged into the agent state using the graph's reducers, updating the agent state accordingly.","citations":["c1","c2"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"The different response_format options that use StructuredResponseT in LangChain are: ToolStrategy[StructuredResponseT], ProviderStrategy[StructuredResponseT], type[StructuredResponseT], and None.","citations":["c1","c2"]},{"text":"ToolStrategy[StructuredResponseT] uses tool calling for structured output.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"ProviderStrategy[StructuredResponseT] uses provider-native structured output.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"type[StructuredResponseT] is a schema type that automatically selects the best strategy based on model capabilities.","citations":["c1","c2"]},{"text":"None means structured output is not explicitly requested.","citations":["c1"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"The store_based_model middleware selects which model to use for a request by reading the user's preferred model from the Store using the user_id from the request's runtime context.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"If the user's preferred model is found in the Store and is present in the predefined MODEL_MAP, the middleware overrides the request's model with the preferred model from MODEL_MAP.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"If no preferred model is found or it is not in MODEL_MAP, the middleware does not change the model and proceeds with the original request model.","citations":["c1"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"To update model profiles using data from models.dev in LangChain, first update the source data at models.dev through a pull request to its GitHub repository if needed.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"Next, update additional fields and overrides in the file langchain_<package>/data/profile_augmentations.toml through a pull request to the LangChain integration package if needed.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"Then, use the langchain-model-profiles CLI tool to pull the latest data from models.dev, merge in the augmentations, and update the profile data by running the command: langchain-profiles refresh --provider <provider> --data-dir <data_dir>.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"This command downloads the latest data for the specified provider from models.dev, merges augmentations from profile_augmentations.toml in the specified data directory, and writes merged profiles to _profiles.py in that directory.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"An example command to refresh profiles for the 'anthropic' provider is: uv run --with langchain-model-profiles langchain-profiles refresh --provider anthropic --data-dir langchain_anthropic/data.","citations":["c5"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"The value function in reasoning_fig7 is used to assess the quality of reasoning steps and to search over multiple reasoning trajectories.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"This approach improves reliability by generating a set of answers and then using the value function to pick the best one, rather than generating a single answer from the model.","citations":["c1"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"The summarization_prompt is a text prompt that instructs the model to summarize an article about an invention following a specific schema.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"It describes the parameters that the summary should include, such as invented_year, summary, inventors, concepts, and description.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"The prompt is used as the system message content in a chat completion request to guide the model's output to match the structured ArticleSummary format.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"This structured summarization approach is useful for transforming text content into a structured object for display or database population.","citations":["c8"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"You can build React UIs for real-time agent interactions using LangChain's frontend streaming capabilities with the @useStream hook.","citations":["c5"]},{"text":"LangChain supports streaming tokens directly from a chat model and streaming agent progress in real-time, which can be integrated into React UIs.","citations":["c5","c7"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"You can trace each step of a conversational loop, debug tool calls, and evaluate agent outputs with LangSmith.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"To get set up for tracing, follow the tracing quickstart guide at /langsmith/trace-with-langchain.","citations":["c1","c2","c5"]},{"text":"It is recommended to also set up LangSmith Engine, which monitors your traces, detects issues, and proposes fixes.","citations":["c1","c2","c5"]},{"text":"Invoke an agent with a message and pass a thread_id so the agent can persist and resume conversation history, enabling tracing of the conversation state.","citations":["c1","c7"]},{"text":"To enable LangSmith tracing, set environment variables LANGSMITH_TRACING=true and LANGSMITH_API_KEY with your API key.","citations":["c6","c8"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"Chat models accept context as a sequence of message objects, which include system instructions and human inputs, forming a growing list of messages over time.","citations":["c1","c2"]},{"text":"Because context windows are limited, applications often use techniques to remove or \"forget\" stale information to manage the growing message list.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"Interactions with chat models are often stateless, so each model invocation involves passing the entire accumulated list of messages as input.","citations":["c2"]},{"text":"Multi-turn agents accumulate long message histories, and tools like LangSmith can record each turn, tool result, and model response for inspection.","citations":["c4"]},{"text":"Model context includes the full list of messages (conversation history) sent to the model, along with system prompts, tools, model configuration, and response format.","citations":["c5"]},{"text":"Transient updates can modify messages sent to the model for a single call without changing saved state, while persistent updates modify the conversation history state using lifecycle hooks or commands.","citations":["c6"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"LangChain standardizes model inputs and outputs to handle different provider-specific APIs and message formats, making it easy for developers to switch between models without lock-in.","citations":["c2","c3"]},{"text":"For structured output, LangChain uses the `response_format` parameter to control how the agent returns structured data, supporting strategies like `ToolStrategy` for tool calling and `ProviderStrategy` for provider-native structured output.","citations":["c4"]},{"text":"When a schema type is provided directly for structured output, LangChain automatically selects `ProviderStrategy` if the model and provider support native structured output (e.g., OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI), otherwise it uses `ToolStrategy`.","citations":["c4"]},{"text":"LangChain normalizes provider-specific streaming formats (such as Anthropic's `thinking` blocks or OpenAI's `reasoning` summaries) into a standard `reasoning` content block type via the `content_blocks` property.","citations":["c6"]},{"text":"Provider-specific content blocks and escape hatches exist as `NonStandardContentBlock` with type `non_standard` to handle experimental or unique provider features.","citations":["c8"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"You can customize a chat model's input size and capabilities by providing a custom model profile dictionary when initializing the chat model, specifying parameters such as 'max_input_tokens', 'tool_calling', and 'structured_output'.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"A custom profile can be passed to the 'init_chat_model' function using the 'profile' parameter to overwrite or update model profile data.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"Chat models accept parameters that configure behavior, including model name, provider, authentication key, randomness (temperature), and maximum tokens for output length.","citations":["c2"]},{"text":"You can create runtime-configurable models by specifying configurable fields such as 'model', 'model_provider', 'temperature', and 'max_tokens', allowing dynamic changes to model parameters.","citations":["c7"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"Defining essential connections in a graph-based system allows nodes to handle their own routing logic, keeping control flow explicit and traceable so the next action is always understandable by looking at the current node.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"Edges define how logic is routed and how the graph decides to stop, with types including normal edges for static routing and conditional edges for dynamic routing, affecting how nodes communicate and control flow proceeds.","citations":["c2"]},{"text":"A node can have multiple outgoing edges, and if so, all destination nodes execute in parallel in the next superstep, influencing control flow concurrency.","citations":["c2"]},{"text":"Choosing one routing mechanism per node—either normal edges or conditional edges/Command—is important to avoid mixed paths that complicate reasoning about graph behavior and control flow.","citations":["c2"]},{"text":"Conditional edges use routing functions that determine which node(s) to route to next after execution, enabling optional routing or termination and thus dynamic control flow.","citations":["c3"]},{"text":"Nodes declare possible next nodes using type hints with Command objects, making routing explicit and traceable, which structures control flow clearly within the graph.","citations":["c4"]},{"text":"Using Command objects in nodes allows combining state updates and routing decisions in a single function, enabling both control flow and state changes to be managed together.","citations":["c5","c8"]},{"text":"Conditional entry points allow starting at different nodes based on custom logic, affecting initial control flow routing in the graph.","citations":["c6"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"A super-step in LangGraph is a single 'tick' of the graph where all nodes scheduled for that step execute, potentially in parallel.","citations":["c1","c2"]},{"text":"In a sequential graph, each node or step corresponds to a separate super-step, producing a checkpoint after each one.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"LangGraph creates a checkpoint at each super-step boundary, which is a full state snapshot that can be used to resume execution.","citations":["c1","c3"]},{"text":"Within a super-step, writes from individual node executions are persisted as tasks, enabling recovery of successful nodes' outputs if another node in the same super-step fails.","citations":["c1","c3"]},{"text":"Execution can only be resumed from a checkpoint at a super-step boundary, not mid-function inside a node.","citations":["c1","c4"]},{"text":"When resuming execution after an interrupt or retry, the affected node runs again from the start of its function, so node logic should be idempotent.","citations":["c4"]}]}

{"insufficient_evidence":false,"claims":[{"text":"The core agent loop involves calling a model, letting it choose tools to execute, and finishing when it calls no more tools.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"A typical agent loop consists of two main steps: 1) Model call - calls the LLM with a prompt and available tools, returns either a response or a request to execute tools; 2) Tool execution - executes the tools that the LLM requested, returns tool results.","citations":["c2"]},{"text":"This loop continues until the LLM decides to finish.","citations":["c2"]},{"text":"Middleware exposes hooks before and after each of the core agent loop steps.","citations":["c1"]},{"text":"Middleware provides two styles of hooks to intercept agent execution: node-style hooks and wrap-style hooks.","citations":["c5"]},{"text":"Node-style hooks run sequentially at specific execution points such as before the agent starts, before each model call, after each model response, and after the agent completes.","citations":["c3"]},{"text":"Wrap-style hooks run around each call, giving control over execution, such as around each model call and around each tool call.","citations":["c3"]},{"text":"Middleware allows hooking into any step in the agent lifecycle to update context (modify state, update conversation history, save insights) or jump in the lifecycle (skip steps or repeat calls based on context).","citations":["c6"]}]}
